title: Worriers May Find Doing Nothing Distressing, Says Study
paragraphs: For many people, having a few minutes with nothing to do is a welcome chance to relax. However, a new study from the United States suggests that for people who tend to worry a lot, sitting idle may actually be distressing.

The study was carried out by researchers at Baylor University in Texas, including Thomas Fergus and Annie Ginty, and it was published in the journal Cognitive Therapy and Research in 2026. According to the researchers, it is the first known study to examine the relationship between worry and what they call "idleness distress."

The researchers carried out three separate studies involving more than 900 participants in total. In the first study, they examined whether people who worry more report feeling greater discomfort when they have nothing to do. In the second, they tested whether people's tendency to worry could predict how distressed they would feel during an idleness task carried out several weeks later. In this task, participants simply sat without being given any instructions. In the third study, the researchers compared the idleness task with a boring task, to see whether worry was linked to distress only when people had nothing at all to do.

Across all three studies, the results were consistent. People who were more likely to worry tended to find doing nothing uncomfortable, distressing or difficult to tolerate. As Ginty explained, not everyone found sitting idle distressing. Instead, the effect was mainly driven by worry.
Fergus suggested that when people have nothing to do, their attention may turn inward, where worries can become more noticeable. As a result, worriers may try to avoid idle moments altogether.

The researchers believe their findings could help develop new ways of treating worry, which is linked to a range of mental and physical health problems. Fergus also suggested that people might learn to deal with unavoidable downtime in different ways.

In addition, the researchers pointed out that constantly using smartphones and other devices may reduce the natural opportunities people have to experience idleness and learn how to cope with it. However, the study did not directly measure smartphone use.
